aAbout: Argos Atlas is a hosted real-time world map that aggregates already-open official feeds — above all public cameras, which it claims number over 200,000 from official portals in more than 190 countries — and paints everything that moves around them on one flat map: flights, ships, war frontlines, verified events, infrastructure, earthquakes, fires and prediction markets. The live map is free with a free account; ARGOS PRO adds recording, history, an AI analyst layer and a 3D globe mode.
aStrengths: Argos Atlas is the deeper working atlas: an order of magnitude more cameras (its claim), camera recording with a 24-hour scrubbable archive, flight and ship history (7–90 days), sanctions and dark-vessel flags, verified frontlines and events, geofence alerts and a 16-camera videowall. It asks nothing of your computer — a free account in any browser — and its team plans (up to 10 seats on DIVISION) aim it at newsrooms and analysts, not just the curious.
bAbout: World Monitor is a free, open-source intelligence dashboard by Elie Habib, published under AGPL-3.0 and hosted at worldmonitor.app. Its homepage, dated 26 October 2026, cites 59 map layer types and 468 news and OSINT feeds spanning geopolitics, conflicts, military movements, markets, shipping, aviation and cyber, correlated onto one live map with AI-synthesised country briefs. It also ships as desktop apps and can be self-hosted from its public source code. No webcam feature appears on its official pages — its cameras are data feeds, not camera streams.
bStrengths: World Monitor is the deeper analysis desk — and the more open one: completely free with no signup, open-source under AGPL-3.0, self-hostable, and also available as native desktop apps. Its dated homepage figures (59 layer types, 468 feeds) cover conflict data, chokepoint tracking, markets and macro sources, fires, quakes and cyber signals, with AI country briefs in the free core and six specialised dashboard variants — geopolitics, tech, finance, energy, commodity and positive news — that Argos does not attempt.
betterAnswer: They solve different problems. Argos Atlas is a hosted, camera-first atlas — 200,000+ cameras claimed, verified events, frontlines and prediction markets — free to open once you create a free account, and paid to record and remember. World Monitor is a free, open-source intelligence dashboard — no signup, no cameras — built to correlate news, conflicts, hazards, aircraft, ships and markets into briefs and scores. If you want to *watch* the world, open Argos Atlas; if you want to *read* it, open World Monitor.

intro: Argos Atlas and World Monitor both promise the whole world on one live map — and they mean very different things by it. Argos Atlas is a hosted website built around public cameras, which it claims number over 200,000 in more than 190 countries, with flights, ships, verified events, 16 frontlines and prediction markets painted around them, free with a free account. World Monitor is a free, open-source (AGPL-3.0) intelligence dashboard by Elie Habib that opens with no signup at all: news and OSINT feeds, conflicts, fires, earthquakes, aircraft, ships and markets — and, on its official pages, no webcams at all.
pricingA: The live atlas is free and, in Argos's words, 'will stay free' — it asks for a free account and shows ads with camera limits. ARGOS PRO (EUR, VAT included in the EU/UK) lists OUTPOST at €15.99/month or €44.99 for 12 months, DISTRICT at €56.99/month or €134.99 for 12 months, DIVISION at €199/month or €809 for 12 months, and AGENCY at €1,049.99/month for registered companies. First-month welcome discounts apply to OUTPOST and DISTRICT; there is no free trial.
pricingB: The dashboard is free at $0 — every map layer except Resilience, with no signup. Pro is $39.99/month or $359.99/year and adds the WM Analyst AI chat, a personal intelligence digest, real-time alerts, the scenario engine and MCP connectors; Pro Business is $49.99/month, and API plans run $99.99/month (API Starter) to $299.99/month (API Business), with Enterprise custom. The AGPL-3.0 source code itself is free to download and self-host.

verdictA: Choose Argos Atlas if cameras are the point — the biggest claimed camera catalogue, recording, history and alerts — plus verified events, frontlines and prediction markets in the same hosted map.
verdictB: Choose World Monitor if you want free, no-signup geopolitical analysis — deep news, conflict, chokepoint and markets panels, AI briefs and open-source code you can self-host — and you do not need live cameras.
verdictLine: Argos Atlas is the camera-first atlas — a hosted map that watches places. World Monitor is the intel dashboard — a free, open-source map that reads events. If you need to see a location, pick Argos; if you need to understand a situation, pick World Monitor.
worldEye: If Argos's account wall is the friction in one, and World Monitor's missing cameras are the gap in the other, WorldEye is the middle path: a hosted globe that opens free in any browser with no signup at all — 74,229 public cameras across 105 countries. It does not claim Argos's 200,000+ camera scale or its recording archive, and it does not match World Monitor's open-source code or its depth of geopolitical panels. Its Pro tier ($7.99/week, $13.99/month or $74.99/year) is priced well under both paid ladders here.
